articles.title: Young people turned out in near-record numbers for the 2026 midterms, with the economy top of their minds
articles.author: Sara Suzuki, Senior Researcher and Research Assistant Professor at CIRCLE, Tufts University
paras: The economy was the top issue for voters in the November 2026 midterm elections, which saw Democrats win decisive majorities in both houses of Congress.

And for young voters, whether in college or not, the economy and jobs, as well as healthcare, were their top concerns, our research at CIRCLE, a nonpartisan, research organization focused on youth civic engagement at Tufts University, shows.

Overall, 27% of young people – meaning people ages 18 to 29 – went to the polls during the midterms, our Nov. 5 analysis shows. This marks the second-highest midterm youth voter turnout in the past 30 years, behind only the 2018 election cycle.

As a scholar at CIRCLE who studies young people and their voting behavior, I think it’s helpful to understand some of the factors that motivated so many young people to vote – and to cast their lot with the Democrats.
Understanding young voters
Among youth, being enrolled as a college student or not did not make a big difference in who they voted for during these midterms.

But there are some voting trend differences based on young people’s educational attainment, especially in the gap between young people with an education level of high school or less, and those with at least some college experience and more. Those with only a high school degree or less voted Democratic by a 24-point margin, compared with a 42-point margin among those with at least some college education.

College students who are young men also voted Democrat by a 24-point margin. Female college students, meanwhile, voted Democrat at a 45-point margin. A similar gender gap appears among young voters who aren’t in college.
Overall, this gender gap has persisted at least since 2024, as young women then were also voting more Democratic than men were.

About 66% of young people ages 18-29 voted for a Democratic candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives, compared with 31% for a Republican candidate, our data shows. This marks the highest percentage of support for Democratic candidates among all age groups.
Within this group, 70% of young women voted for a Democratic U.S. House candidate in the midterms, as opposed to 59% of young men.
Partisan trends among young voters have fluctuated over the past few decades – in 2000, for example, 49% of young people voted Democratic, while 48% voted Republican.

In 2026, Asian American and Pacific Islander, Black and Latino young people gave Democrat candidates the strongest support, at 81%, 79% and 71%, respectively. By comparison, 61% of white young people voted for Democratic House candidates, with 36% voting Republican.
Young people are focused on the economy
Across race, education, income and geographic location, young people overwhelmingly indicated that the economy and jobs was their top issue in this election.
Healthcare and the Iran war also showed up as areas of importance for young voters. All three of these issues are connected to young people’s concerns about the cost of living.
We found that voting preferences did vary according to how young people viewed their own financial circumstances, a pattern that held among college students.
Low-income students were more likely than their affluent peers to vote for Democrats.
The issues that matter most to young people have shifted considerably over the past several years.
In 2020, we were seeing different groups of young people prioritize social issues like racism, climate change and gun control.
In 2022, we began to see young people prioritize the economy – their concern about inflation was the second-most important issue to them after abortion.

Now, after the economy, healthcare was ranked second for young voters. The third-most important issue was the war in Iran. This is striking, because in the past, we’ve polled young voters about foreign policy issues like the war between Israel and Palestinians and the war between Russia and Ukraine. Young people have never really ranked these other foreign policy issues as a top area of concern.

Youth voter turnout generally tends to be much weaker in midterm elections than in presidential elections. In 2018, there was 28% turnout for young people – a midterm turnout that was considerably higher than 2014, when only 13% of young people turned out to vote.

Campaigns seem to recognize that young voters tend to be less politically engaged. For example, our research shows that during the 2024 presidential election cycle, more than 1 in 3 young people were never contacted about the election. Among those without college experience, 48% were never contacted.
Our research still shows that college students face logistical barriers to voting.

Young people are frequent movers, which means they might need to reregister whenever they change addresses. The fact that college students may be living on campus while they’re registered to vote from their parents’ address can also create complications.

College students still have more voting information than young people who are not in college. But compared with other age groups, young people receive less voting information – making their turnout in the 2026 midterms all the more remarkable.

articles.title: I research play – and here’s why recess is much more important than just a fun break
articles.author: Louisa Penfold, Professor of Education, Harvard University
paras: School recess has long been considered a standard part of children’s education in the United States. But it’s more than just a fun break from sitting at a desk.
Daily recess is necessary for supporting young children and adolescents’ learning, as well as their physical and mental health.

It’s so important that the American Academy of Pediatrics notes that reducing the amount of time set aside for playing, running and exploring in order to fit in more academic work could actually be counterproductive.
But in recent decades many schools have cut back on recess, which many states do not require.

As a scholar who researches childhood play, I have studied and witnessed the benefits of play in children’s lives, including the significant social, emotional and cognitive impacts it has on students’ overall well-being.
The many benefits of recess
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that children and adolescents get at least 60 minutes of physical activity per day.
The CDC also defines recess as a “regularly scheduled period in the school day for physical activity and play that is monitored by trained staff or volunteers.”
Recess can look different across various schools – while some kids play outside on play structures or in grassy fields, others might play indoors during inclement weather.
Research also shows, for example, that children living in lower-income communities have fewer opportunities than their peers in higher-income communities to play outside.
Unlike physical education classes or participating in organized sports, recess gives students the time to engage in physical activity and interact with their peers however they like.

This time for unstructured play can offer much-needed relief from the mental focus that students need to maintain throughout the school day. It can also support their cognitive development and overall emotional and physical well-being.
Research also consistently shows that giving children breaks each day for recess has immense benefits for their mental health and the executive functioning skills that support academic achievement.
This includes benefits for students’ focus and creativity, as well as their memory and executive function.
Some states, but not all, require recess
Most states do not mandate that schools have recess every day or spell out a minimum amount of time students must spend moving their bodies.

A 2025 report from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health found that 11 states have laws addressing school recess. This ranges from Arizona’s requirement for 40 minutes of daily recess to Georgia, Indiana and Kentucky all requiring recess, but with no minimum duration.

Massachusetts is one of the nearly 40 states without any laws regarding recess time. A recent article in The Boston Globe reported schools in Cambridge having 25 minutes of recess, while other schools across the state had only 15 minutes per day.

Overall, there has been an uptick in state legislation aimed at preserving mandated daily school recess time, thanks partly to a new parent-led advocacy group called Say Yes to Recess. This group is pushing for schools across the country to provide a minimum of 60 minutes of protected school recess time each day.
Started by three Tennessee moms, Say Yes to Recess has also helped advocate for Tennessee legislation that increased the state’s mandated daily school recess time from 15 to 40 minutes in July 2025.
During the 2001-02 school year, elementary school students from 349 school districts spent on average 36.8 minutes per day at recess.
By 2025, the CDC found that students were spending 27 minutes on average in recess each day.
It’s also hard to track how much physical activity students get at school because public school districts and private schools often do not record and report this information.

While the benefits of recess are not just isolated to young children, a 2026 international study showed that the amount of daily recess time across U.S. schools declines from a mean of 39.3 minutes per day for 6- to 7-year-olds to 24.5 minutes per day for 12- to 18-year-olds.
I conducted research at the Project Zero research center for creativity, ethics and the arts at Harvard University and highlighted the significance of play and the arts within urban public schools.

This 2024 study showed how play with materials supports both children’s and teachers’ creative learning. As someone who designs and studies children’s play spaces, I worry about what could happen if schools continue to reduce school recess because of staffing issues, budget cuts or prioritization of students’ preparation for high-stakes tests focused solely on literacy and numeracy.
Research shows that this trend of not prioritizing recess could have significant effects on children’s and adolescents’ mental health, cognitive development and overall enjoyment of school.
School are well intended but under strain

The decline in time for recess comes at a moment when many schools and districts are under increasing pressure as a result of declining student enrollment, pressure to meet state learning standards and budget cuts.
For some schools, reduced staffing and the costs of maintaining outdoor play equipment to meet safety requirements have made it difficult to offer school recess.
For other schools, an assumption that more time for instruction equals a higher-quality education may be driving decisions to minimize or eliminate time for unstructured play.
Another factor that influences recess is when schools deny students recess time as a form of punishment – a policy that some scholars and educators are trying to block through legislation.

As childhood health, social and cognitive research demonstrates, the amount of time school recess is given matters in children’s development as whole human beings. I believe it is up to schools, districts and parents to advocate for and ensure children’s right to protected school recess time every day.
Harvard Graduate School of Education Project Zero at the Harvard Graduate School of Education

articles.title: An ADHD diagnosis can be a map to guide a person through challenging territory – not to avoid it altogether
articles.author: Deldhy Nicolás Moya Sánchez, Psychiatrist and Consultation-Liaison Psychiatry, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM)
paras: Picture a young person who walks out of my office with a new ADHD diagnosis and feels relief. There is finally a name for years of missed deadlines and unfinished paperwork.
A few weeks later, they use that name to end an argument at home about an unmade bed and a pile of unopened mail, saying, “I can’t do that, I have ADHD.”

In another scenario, a student asks me for a medical note excusing them from a written assignment. Not extra time, not a quieter room, not help breaking the work into steps: They want the assignment dropped.

I often see both situations in my Mexico City clinic. They raise the same question: Does a diagnosis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder explain why a task is harder? Usually, yes. Does it settle which tasks the person should stop attempting? Rarely.

I am a liaison psychiatrist at the National Medical Center “20 de Noviembre” in Mexico City and a professor of medicine at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. My work deals with how psychiatric diagnoses land in a person’s daily life, including how anxiety and ADHD can mask each other. I sign several of those school and work notes every week.
Researchers have started to measure something I see constantly in the clinic: how much room a diagnosis takes up in how a person sees themselves.

Used as a map, a diagnosis shows where the difficult ground is and the best route through it. For instance, mornings may be when a patient falls apart, so we plan for them: medication, more structure and a few skills to practice. Used as an alibi – an excuse to avoid blame – a diagnosis marks the whole territory as off-limits.
Research suggests these two uses lead to very different lives: one in which someone gets through the day and another that shrinks around the diagnosis.
When the label takes up all the room
Psychologists who study chronic illness use the term “illness identity” for how far a diagnosis gets folded into a person’s sense of self.

A Belgian study of adolescents and young adults who have Type 1 diabetes described four ways a person can relate to a diagnosis: rejection, which is acting as though the diagnosis is not there; acceptance, which is “this is part of me, but only part”; enrichment, which is “it taught me something”; and engulfment, which is when it overshadows everything else.

Engulfment is high when someone can no longer describe who they are, what they want or what they are good at without the diagnosis taking precedence. The condition stops being something they have and becomes how they define themselves.

In 2025, an Israeli team surveyed 154 adolescents with ADHD about how much their diagnosis had shaped their sense of self. The researchers found that how engulfed participants felt predicted their quality of life more strongly than how severe their symptoms were. Of the four patterns, engulfment was the only one that explained why more severe symptoms coincided with a worse life.

The same research group found a similar pattern in a second study. In 66 adolescents, the more the diagnosis had taken over, the worse participants did on executive functioning, self-management and quality of life measures – in plain terms: planning ahead, starting a task and running their own routines.

These are snapshots, not experiments. They show that self-identity and well-being are linked, but they cannot tell us which one is driving the other. Even so, the pattern matches what parents describe to me as the moment their child stops saying “This is hard for me” and starts saying “This is what I am.”
‘It’s my brain’ can dampen effort
The brain differences in people with ADHD are real. Yet the way clinicians, teachers and parents explain a diagnosis can feed a disempowering loop.

Meta-analyses pool the results of many studies. One, co-authored by University of Melbourne psychologists, found that when a mental health problem is explained in biological terms – as a matter of genes or brain chemistry – blame goes down, which is good.
But a second meta-analysis, by another group of psychologists from Melbourne, found that brain-based explanations raise pessimism about recovery, which is not good.
The same explanation that lifts the blame can also lower the expectation of change.
Avoiding something usually makes it more threatening

One type of support can keep someone engaged with a task they find hard: an essay broken into steps with a deadline for each one, or a teacher who checks in at the start of a lesson rather than at the end. Another kind can take the task away.
The first builds skill. The second teaches that the task really is impossible.

Researchers who study childhood anxiety call that second kind “family accommodation,” and they mean something specific: A household gradually reorganizes itself so the child never has to face what frightens them. Someone answers the phone for the teenager who dreads phone calls, or the family stops having people over because visitors make the child anxious.

In schools, “accommodation” means something else: a change to the setting, such as extra time or a quieter room, so the student can still do the task. To avoid confusion, I call this school version “support.”

Nobody is asking families to be harsher or less understanding. But a Spanish meta-analysis found that the pattern of removing the feared situation is linked to more severe anxiety in children and adolescents.

A randomized trial showed that treating only the parents worked as well as treating the child. Parents were taught to respond supportively while stepping back from rescuing their child from what frightened them.

Teachers and school staff can also steer students away from hard tasks, often without realizing it. When a panel of experts reviewed school supports given to 76 anxious students in treatment, some pushed the student toward the difficult task and others pushed them away from it. Students with social anxiety most often got the ones that let them skip exactly what they feared: being seen and heard by their classmates.
Support and treatment are not the same thing

Educational supports are by far the most common response to ADHD in schools. Many families ask me for a letter requesting extra time on exams. One study found improved reading comprehension for college students with ADHD – but about as much improvement for their peers without the disorder. So extra time helps, but not the way a treatment does.

Most supports show no benefit specific to students with the disorder. That does not make them useless; several help any student. It means they are not treatment: A student can have numerous supports for years while the attention problem stays where it was.

After a diagnosis, the practical work focuses on medication, therapy, structure and a list of tasks that are broken down into smaller parts. I hand every patient that list, written down, before they leave.
Where this leaves the person in my office

When I write a school or work note, three things belong in it. First, the specific task the person struggles with. Second, the support that keeps them engaged with that task rather than away from it. Third, a date to review it: a support nobody looks at again stops being a clinical decision and becomes a permanent feature of someone’s life.
A good diagnosis does not remove responsibility. It moves it. The question stops being: “Why can’t I?” Rather, it becomes: “What do I work on, and with what help?”
The young person who learned to say “I can’t, I have ADHD” is not wrong about the diagnosis. They just have the rest of the sentence left to write.

articles.title: Are schools a great equalizer? They help kids catch up, but wealthier children still pull ahead
articles.author: David Blazar, Malen Professor for Urban Education Policy, University of Maryland
paras: In 1848, the education reformer Horace Mann called public schooling “the great equalizer of the conditions of men.” More than 175 years later, education scholars are still arguing about whether he was right.

Some research finds that a child’s family background shapes their academic achievement far more than schools do. Other work finds that schools narrow academic achievement gaps that would otherwise be even wider.

A classic study following Baltimore children in the 1980s found that low-income and wealthier kids learned at similar rates during the school year. Achievement gaps grew over the summer, when some children read with parents, visited libraries and went to camp, while others didn’t have those same opportunities. How much summer learning loss exists is still an open question.

But the larger point holds: Gaps between rich and poor children in reading and math skills are already large on the first day of kindergarten, driven by factors outside of K-12 schooling. For a given group of students, those gaps then stay about the same size through the school years.
I am a scholar of education policy who studies the different factors that shape students’ learning, including teachers and the quality of their instruction.

Instead of measuring how much students learn at school, as is often the case, my colleagues and I recently measured what students receive in and out of school: the school funding, education support services and time that schools, government programs and families put into each child.
By some measures, schools really are an equalizer for children from different backgrounds – but this finding has its limits.
A gap that starts early in childhood

In our 2026 study, we combined data from 10 nationally representative government surveys to track 77 kinds of investments, as we call them, that contribute to raising and educating children. This includes teachers, tutoring, housing, food and childcare. We also measured factors that don’t have a direct cost, such as the time parents and caregivers spend reading with children.
We put a dollar value on each factor – valuing parents’ time at the average U.S. hourly wage, for example – so we could add them up and compare what children from different backgrounds receive.
Counting government investment, family spending and the time parents spend with their children, the average child in the U.S. receives about US$502,000 from birth to age 18, our analysis shows.
The gaps in how much different children receive start early.
Before age 5, children from the poorest fourth of families receive about $44,000 less in total investments than children from the richest fourth – marking a gap of 24%.
Most of that early difference comes from housing and childcare costs.
However, a striking pattern emerges as children transition into elementary school. The gap in total investment between the richest and poorest children is cut in half, from 24% to 12%.
For Black children, the benefit of starting school is even greater. Investment gaps between Black and white children shrink from 20% in early childhood years to 7% once kindergarten begins.
This matters because research shows that more school spending improves students’ achievement and long-term outcomes, especially for those from low-income families.
So why don’t achievement gaps close during the school years?
Catching up vs. getting ahead
Part of the answer is what money buys.

Our research shows that once children are in school, those from the lowest-income families receive 72% more in tutoring and 68% more in special education than those from the highest-income families, and Black children receive more than twice as much tutoring as white children.
These services are meant to help students catch up. A dollar spent catching up is not the same as a dollar spent getting ahead.

Tutoring has long been one of schools’ main catch-up tools, and since the pandemic, schools have leaned on it more than ever. It’s a reasonable bet. Studies that randomly assign students to tutoring find some of the largest test-score gains of any school program.

Schools serving many low-income students have long been able to use federal Title I money for tutoring. Pandemic relief money made a bigger push possible. Congress sent schools nearly $190 billion, and the largest round was divided among districts the same way as Title I money, so high-poverty districts got more.

By 2022-23, more than a third of public schools offered “high-dosage” tutoring, meaning frequent sessions in small groups. Schools serving more low-income students and students of color were more likely to offer it.
But for many low-income, Black and Latino students, tutoring wasn’t new.

In our data, collected from 2014 to 2021, about 17% of school-age children were being tutored, including 25% of Black children and 19% of Latino children, compared with 14% of white children. For Black, Latino and low-income children who received tutoring, over 75% got that support from public schools.

Early in the recovery, at least, the share of students getting tutoring didn’t appear to grow much. A nationally representative survey of parents in fall 2022 found about 15% of students were being tutored.

Meanwhile, the pandemic widened achievement gaps. Students in high-poverty districts still trail those in wealthier districts by more than students in the same grades did before the pandemic. Schools leaned harder on catch-up help that low-income, Black and Latino students were already getting. Federal relief money did help high-poverty districts recover. But even with that help, gaps remain wider than before the pandemic.
Catch-up help is only half the picture. Wealthier children also get more of the resources that help them pull ahead, in school and out.

Some studies show, for example, that low-income students and students of color are more likely than richer, white students to have newer, less experienced teachers. Our study documents the same pattern.
The differences are even starker outside of school.
In our data, wealthier families invest far more in music lessons, sports and other activities that can help kids get ahead.

Related research shows that by 2024, the richest 10% of families spent more than 13 times as much per child as the poorest quarter on childcare, education and extracurricular activities – up from about three times as much in the early 1980s.
Equal spending isn’t enough
Our findings show that public education is the main reason the investment gap between rich and poor children shrinks once kids turn 5.

But equal spending is not equal opportunity. Much of the extra school spending on low-income, Black and Latino children goes to making up for gaps that opened before they started school. Meanwhile, wealthier children keep getting more of the experienced teachers and enrichment that help them pull ahead.

If schools are going to be a true equalizer – closing gaps, not just keeping them from growing – more catch-up help won’t be enough on its own. These students also need more of what helps their wealthier peers get ahead. And because the widest gaps open before kindergarten – in housing and childcare, where public support is thinnest – closing them can’t be left to schools alone.
David Blazar received funding from the Spencer Foundation to conduct the analyses described in this article.

articles.title: Nearly 7 in 10 professors report being bullied, often by students over grades
articles.author: Jason Walker, Associate Professor of Psychology, Health and Wellness, Adler University
paras: Faculty and university staff members report being bullied in two ways: by their colleagues and supervisors, and by their students over grades, according to an international study I conducted with colleagues Zahra Moradi and Deborah Circo.

Researchers define workplace bullying as harmful acts of mistreatment between people that go beyond incivility and cross the line to intentionally cause harm. In other words, it’s behavior any reasonable person would know isn’t OK.
Junior faculty and staff faced more workplace bullying from peers. Faculty members and staff who are Black, Indigenous or people of color were targeted more frequently.

Senior faculty were more likely than younger educators to report being bullied by students over grades. Although bullying usually runs down the chain of power – for example, from a boss to an employee – grade bullying flips that. Researchers call it contrapower harassment – when someone with less formal power targets someone with more.
More than 30% of adult workers in the U.S. and Canada experience bullying, harassment and sexual abuse in the workplace at any given time, harming both individuals and organizations.

That rate is more than double in academia, where bullying rates are as high as 68% at some institutions, far exceeding those in general workplaces and aligning with high-stress fields like emergency services, according to our peer-reviewed findings published in the October 2026 Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Practice.
Academic bullying undermines both the well-being of staff and faculty and the integrity of higher education institutions.

Thirty percent of our survey respondents reported that students pressured them for a better grade. Students’ tactics included threatening grade appeals, malicious complaints, negative online reviews, emotional manipulation and intimidation. Women and minority faculty are particularly affected. Over time, the bullying creates a toxic environment that damages relationships between faculty and students and hurts the quality of education for everyone.

Such pressure could result in mental health issues like anxiety and depression, decreased job satisfaction and reduced productivity. These dynamics not only affect individual faculty members but can also lead to long-term damage to the reputation of institutions and negatively impact students’ educational experiences.
We surveyed 189 faculty and staff at colleges and universities in Canada, the U.S. and U.K.
Anonymous respondents reported how often they’d faced 22 common forms of mistreatment from colleagues and supervisors. A separate set of questions asked about pressure from students over grades.
The most common issues related to colleagues weren’t shouting or threats. They were easier to dismiss: unmanageable workloads, withheld information and impossible deadlines.
Pressure from students over grades was reported more frequently than bullying from colleagues.
Gaps remain in understanding the root causes of bullying of faculty.

Studies that follow the same faculty over several years could show how grade bullying builds over time, and whether it pushes people to leave or lose trust in their institutions. One likely pattern is that grade bullying escalates when it works, wearing faculty down until they either give in or leave their jobs.
Researchers need to test what actually works to stop bullying, and whether those fixes hold up at different kinds of colleges and universities.
Bigger studies would help. So would sitting down with faculty and hearing their experiences in their own words to add context that a survey can’t capture.
Future research could also explore interventions to mitigate bullying and measure their effectiveness across diverse educational contexts.

Bullying at work is a form of violence. The harm is psychological rather than physical, but it’s real. Change starts with higher standards of conduct for everyone, from first-year students to senior administrators and leaders committed to enforcing respectful rules.
The Research Brief is a short take on interesting academic work.

articles.title: Students who attended Miami-Dade public school pre-K outperformed peers in 18-year study
articles.author: Charles Bleiker, Associate Professor of Early Childhood Education, Florida International University
paras: Choosing a preschool is a difficult and important decision. Parents are weighing cost, proximity and convenience with how each program meets the needs of the child and matches the goals and values of their family and cultural community.

This choice makes a difference. Research in early education clearly shows that children who attend high-quality preschool programs – those with smaller class sizes, a developmentally appropriate curriculum, warm teacher-child interactions and established, efficient routines – are better prepared for kindergarten.

We are researchers who study early childhood education, and we conducted an 18-year study tracking the academic progress of 27,814 students who attended different types of prekindergarten in Miami and then went on to attend the Miami-Dade County Public Schools system from kindergarten through high school. We found that the type of pre-K program the children attended made a difference for their overall educational outcomes.

From 2002 to 2007, we partnered with Miami-Dade County Public Schools, early childcare providers across the county and the Early Learning Coalition of Miami-Dade, a nonprofit that works with childcare providers and communities to promote school readiness, with the goal of assessing five cohorts of about 10,000 students per year.

School readiness takes into consideration the children’s cognitive, language, motor and social skills, as well as behavior problems. During the study, we shared the data we collected with parents, teachers and center directors to inform interventions for struggling kids and improvements to their pre-K programs.

Some of the students in these five cohorts attended taxpayer-funded, public school pre-K programs, while some received federal subsidies administered through the state of Florida to attend center-based or family childcare at age 4.

Center-based programs, like a Kiddie Academy, for example, can be nonprofit or for-profit centers in the community. They operate either in a freestanding location or as part of a corporate or faith-based building. Family or home-based childcare programs are generally smaller and operate out of private residences.

After the children had moved through pre-K, we continued to receive their anonymized academic records each year, as long as they stayed in the public school system. The last cohort of students completed 12th grade in spring 2020.

We found that children who attended public school pre-K programs at age 4 achieved the strongest third-grade outcomes on standardized reading and math test scores and GPA. These children outperformed those who attended center-based care, who in turn generally performed better than children who were enrolled in family childcare. Kids who attended public school pre-K were 35% less likely to be held back in third grade compared with the other groups.
Further, we found that kids who attended higher-quality elementary schools – as measured by the Florida Department of Education – did better on average.

However, the quality of the elementary school that students went on to attend didn’t change the differences we observed across the early childhood education types, except when it came to reading skills. Students who attended center-based care and went on to attend higher-quality schools were better able to catch up to the public school pre-K kids by third grade in reading.

Our findings are consistent with most previous studies of public pre-K. Students who attended public pre-K programs in Boston; Tulsa, Oklahoma; and North Carolina have shown better results on standardized test scores, lower absenteeism and better grade retention when compared with children who attended other programs, even as late as eighth grade.

However, there are outliers. Children who attended the publicly funded voluntary pre-K program in Tennessee did not perform any better than other children on third or sixth grade outcomes – and in some cases, they performed worse.
Previous findings are also mixed on whether these effects persist past the third grade.

In our study, it appears that the long-term benefits of public school pre-K extend through eighth grade, but this conclusion is still in peer review and has not been published yet. We are currently examining whether benefits persist throughout high school.

Why did kids in public school pre-K programs do better compared to center-based and family childcare? We believe that the answer likely lies in the quality and organizational differences between the three different types of early care and education.

The public school pre-K programs in our study benefited from the collective resources of the fourth-largest public school system in the country. This matters for everything from the quality of teachers they are able to hire to the facilities and curriculum.

Miami-Dade public schools require teachers to have at minimum a bachelor’s degree and a teaching credential, whereas the others required less education at the time of our study. Public pre-K teachers’ certification allows them to teach from pre-K to third grade, so they typically bring their experience of teaching in kindergarten and the early elementary grades to the pre-K classroom.

These programs also used a developmentally appropriate curriculum, while the others used a variety of materials and approaches. When we began this study, the center-based programs were mostly independent, unaffiliated sites, although some for-profits had more than one center in the study, and some nonprofit organizations such as Catholic Charities or the YMCA oversaw multiple centers.

Many of the children in the study moved from one school to another within the same district. Because Miami-Dade’s public schools are part of a countywide system, the children’s academic records moved with them easily, so their new teacher could see their progress. And since the curriculum was the same across the district, the students were able to pick up at their new school where they’d left off.

This continuity could also explain why children who entered the public school system in pre-K performed better than those outside it. The majority of the children in the study went on to attend public elementary school. The kids in public school preschool and their parents were therefore already familiar with the schools that they would be attending the following year. It’s not hard to see how this would be an advantage for a child transitioning from preschool to kindergarten.

Our findings do not indicate to us, however, that every child must attend public school pre-K in order to succeed in school later on. The reality in Miami-Dade County – and in most communities – is that we need all forms of early care and education, and each setting serves important needs for families.

Indeed, students in all three types of programs made excellent school readiness gains from the beginning to the end of the age-4 academic year. It was just that the children in the public school preschools made stronger gains.

Center- and home-based care in Miami-Dade County is much higher quality across the board today than when we began our study back in 2002. Many more centers are accredited, and teacher education levels have improved. In fact, in our assessment, the quality of early education in Miami-Dade County has never been better.

Still, the cohesive system offered by public schools remains the gold standard for preschool when serving most children and families. In terms of teacher preparation and qualifications, standardized curriculum, oversight and alignment with the kindergarten curriculum, public school pre-k for low-income families in Miami still offers the best hope of long-term academic success.

articles.title: How moving civil rights enforcement out of the US Department of Education threatens students’ protections from race, sex and disability discrimination
articles.author: Bridget Joyce, Director of Programming at Education Rights Institute, University of Virginia
paras: Many people are not familiar with the Office for Civil Rights, an office within the U.S. Department of Education that enforces statutes that protect students from discrimination. So, it might help to consider a recent example of this office’s work.

In December 2022, the Office for Civil Rights, or OCR, found that Ottumwa Community School District, about 90 miles southeast of Des Moines, Iowa, had violated Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 by failing to address racial harassment. Title VI bars schools receiving federal funds from discriminating based on race, color or national origin.

The harassment was so severe that the office found that the student “was subjected to a racially hostile environment.” OCR also found that the school and district “failed to address the pervasive racial harassment of which it was aware.”

The harassment spanned two school years, during which that student was called “blackie,” “slave,” “cotton picker” and other racial slurs. One white student knelt on a Gatorade bottle and said, “It can’t breathe,” mocking the murder of George Floyd, according to the complaint.

Ottumwa Community School District entered a resolution agreement with OCR and agreed to reimburse the student’s family for therapy. The district also agreed to train students and staff on nondiscrimination policies, among other actions.

We spent a combined 17 years at the U.S. Department of Education – one of us in the Office of the General Counsel from 1999 to 2004 and the other in OCR from 2013 to 2025. We saw firsthand the pivotal role that OCR plays in protecting students’ civil rights.

In June 2026, the Trump administration announced a new interagency agreement that provides a way to shift OCR’s day-to-day civil rights enforcement responsibilities from the Department of Education to the Department of Justice.

The administration has not released details on whether OCR has begun to transfer enforcement responsibilities to the Department of Justice under the June 2026 interagency agreement or what, exactly, that would look like.
But this reorganization may mean that most complaints filed with OCR will never be investigated, and those that are could take years to resolve.
In fiscal year 2024 – October 2023 through September 2024 – OCR received over 22,000 complaints related to discrimination based on race, color, national origin, sex and disability.

Individuals and families who file complaints with OCR may want to avoid the expense of filing a lawsuit in a federal court or to secure relief for a student more quickly than a federal court can provide it.

OCR typically seeks to resolve any violations of the laws that it enforces through voluntary resolution agreements, initiating proceedings to terminate federal funding to school districts only when voluntary resolution is not possible, which has historically been rare.
The Department of Education and Department of Justice announced in June 2026 that they had entered an interagency agreement to “deepen their partnership to secure equal access to education.”
Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon explained that the Department of Justice would handle OCR’s complaints “from soup to nuts,” taking on “99 percent” of that work.
This is another step toward the Trump administration’s 2025 promise to close the Department of Education, though only Congress can do that.
Moving the Office for Civil Rights’ enforcement responsibilities to the Department of Justice will significantly change how Title VI and other federal civil rights laws are enforced in schools.

The Department of Justice’s Educational Opportunities Section has long jointly enforced most of the laws that OCR enforces, with each agency generally separately handling its own cases under these laws.
However, there are a few important distinctions between how OCR and the Department of Justice enforce civil rights laws.
Not the same kind of federal response

First, the Office for Civil Rights is legally required to consider every complaint that it receives. It also must promptly investigate complaints that show possible violations of federal civil rights laws.

A January 2026 Government and Accountability Office report found that OCR dismissed about 90% of complaints for part of 2025, raising questions about whether OCR was dismissing complaints without full review during that time. Historically, however, we have seen OCR comply with the requirement to consider all complaints.

In contrast, the Department of Justice’s Educational Opportunities Section selects only a small fraction of cases to pursue, usually tackling systemic or particularly severe discrimination in federal courts.
Both agencies carry out important civil rights work.

But shifting OCR’s enforcement responsibilities to the Department of Justice will mean that students lose their guarantee that a federal agency will review and evaluate their allegations that a school district violated their civil rights.
A different approach to civil rights enforcement
Another distinction is that the Office for Civil Rights typically resolves complaints on its own, without involving federal courts.
OCR has traditionally aimed to resolve complaints within 180 days of receipt, because unresolved discrimination hinders students’ ability to learn.
It can sometimes take longer than this to reach a resolution. Between October 2023 and September 2024, for example, OCR did not resolve approximately 30% of the complaints received within 180 days.
In contrast, the Department of Justice’s Educational Opportunities Section can sometimes take years to resolve its cases in court.
Department of Justice cannot handle OCR’s caseload
A third distinction is that the Department of Justice’s Educational Opportunities Section is not staffed to handle the volume of civil rights complaints that the Office for Civil Rights receives.
From October 2023 through September 2024, OCR received a record high of 22,687 complaints and employed just under 600 full-time equivalent employees.
OCR investigations and resolutions were still backlogged during the early 2020s.
The number of complaints filed with OCR climbed even higher between October 2024 and September 2025.
The Department of Education reported there were 446 staff employed at OCR in November 2025.

In contrast, the Department of Justice’s Educational Opportunities Section employed about 40 lawyers in January 2025 and had lost the majority of its staff by June 2025. The Educational Opportunities Section has not published a more recent estimate of its staffing.
Chronic understaffing at OCR
Even before the Trump administration, OCR was held back by inadequate funding.
The number of civil rights complaints submitted to OCR has skyrocketed over the past decade, but staffing has not kept pace.
In the early 1980s there was about one staff member for every three new complaints filed at OCR.
By 2024 that ratio had increased to one staff member for every 39 new complaints filed.
During the Biden administration, Congress denied repeated requests from the White House to increase funding to OCR.
Civil rights under the Trump administration

Since January 2025, the administration has closed seven of OCR’s 12 regional offices. The administration also tried to lay off approximately half of OCR’s workforce in March 2025, with additional layoffs in October, but withdrew those layoffs following successful legal challenges.
OCR reached resolution agreements in less than 1% of pending cases in 2025, down from 5% in 2024, according to findings from a U.S. Senate committee report chaired by Sen. Bernie Sanders.

That 1% focused heavily on the administration’s enforcement priorities, such as ending transgender students’ use of restrooms consistent with their gender identity. It did not include a single resolution agreement resolving a complaint of sexual harassment, restraint or seclusion, racial harassment or discriminatory student discipline.
We believe these actions have severely hamstrung OCR’s effectiveness and undermined students’ access to traditional civil rights protections.

These changes raise troubling questions about how and whether a complaint like the one lodged against Ottumwa Community School District would be resolved if it were filed today. They also prompt serious concerns about our nation’s commitment to guaranteeing equal educational opportunity.

Bridget Joyce is the Director of Programming at the Education Rights Institute at the University of Virginia School of Law. She previously worked at the U.S. Department of Education Office for Civil Rights. The Education Rights Institute receives funding from the W.K. Kellogg Foundation.

Kimberly Robinson serves as the Director of the Education Rights Institute and the White Burkett Miller Professor of Law and Public Affairs at the University of Virginia School of Law. Kimberly Robinson formerly served in the U.S. Department of Education’s Office of the General Counsel. The Education Rights Institute receives funding from the W.K. Kellogg Foundation.

articles.title: Philadelphia’s Academy of Natural Sciences just closed – a blow for budding young scientists like me
articles.author: Lili Mei Granda Argianas, Ph.D. Student in Physics, Washington University in St. Louis
paras: When I was a freshman in college at Villanova University outside Philadelphia, I visited the Academy of Natural Sciences for the first time.

My friends who were Philly natives were my tour guides, and I was inspired by their passion for the exhibits. I listened not only to the facts they shared about the museum, but also their childhood stories surrounding it.

As a kid, I remember going to the American Museum of Natural History in New York City and looking up at the massive dinosaur displays. I wondered how creatures as big as those used to walk the same ground as me. My favorite exhibit was the Hall of Ocean Life, where behind the staircase you see a dark, unlit diorama of a giant squid attached to a sperm whale.
The museum gave my curiosity a place to grow.

Now, as a Ph.D. student in physics, I research black holes, with the goal of one day becoming a professor and mentoring students. I was shocked when I heard the news that the Academy of Natural Sciences would be closing.
Over 200 years of hands-on science

Founded in 1812, the Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia is the country’s oldest natural science museum. For two centuries, it has played a vital role in scientific research, education and public engagement. The academy’s research centered heavily on biodiversity, evolution, paleontology and environmental science. In 2011, Drexel University acquired the academy and manages its endowment.

The academy had offered a range of experiences, from the Dinosaur Hall to its butterfly garden, and provided generations of visitors with opportunities to explore science beyond classrooms and textbooks.

On Sept. 1, 2026, however, Drexel University abruptly announced that the museum would close by the end of the month, citing financial difficulties and declining attendance. The last day it was open to visitors was Sept. 27, 2026.

Critics of the decision to close are rallying to “Save the Academy” and reopen it. Even members of the Philadelphia City Council expressed surprise that they had not been approached for support before the closing was announced.

The William Penn Foundation offered to cover operating subsidies for at least another year, potentially giving the academy time to explore a sustainable future. However, the museum remains closed for now, and Drexel maintains it needs a long-term financial solution. At a hearing on Oct. 26 that lasted nearly four hours, Philadelphia City Council members tried to understand why the museum closed and what Drexel would need to reopen it. The hearing is scheduled to resume on Nov. 16.
Cultivating future scientists
While museums may be viewed simply as sites for school field trips or family outings, their impact extends far beyond entertainment.

Natural science museums preserve scientific history through linking the past to future generations, supporting research and introducing young people to subjects they might otherwise never encounter. Philly kids who visited the academy could experience different ecosystems, from the snowy lands of the bobcat to rainforests home to giant monkeys. These dioramas are a snapshot in time that allow children to cultivate their own imagination and passions.

Not everyone has the opportunity to attend college or pursue a career in STEM. Museums help close that gap, giving families, students and children a chance to experience science firsthand – something that textbooks, social media and even classrooms sometimes cannot do.

Thinking back to my own childhood, I can pinpoint how my academic interests were fostered through museums, whether gazing up at galaxies at the Hayden Planetarium or sleeping under the belly of the blue whale in the Hall of Ocean Life. I was able to talk to real scientists in careers I dreamed to achieve, and I was told it was possible for me.
These experiences were integral to my becoming a first-generation college student and pursuing a career in academia. They made a career in science feel tangible rather than mystical or intimidating.

articles.title: What the Cornell 7 sexual assault allegations reveal about how parents talk to their kids about rape
articles.author: Kathleen J Fitzgerald, Teaching Associate Professor of Sociology, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
paras: There is approximately 60 years of research on campus sexual assault and shelves full of books on young people’s sexual experiences and behaviors, including their experiences with assault.

More is likely to be generated following the September 2026 high-profile lawsuit by a female former Cornell University student, known as Jane Doe, who says that a group of seven Chi Phi fraternity members drugged and gang-raped her when she was a sophomore in 2024.
Yet, there is very little research about the role parents have played, or should play, in educating their children about campus sexual assault prevention.
I am a sociologist who spent 2024 and 2025 interviewing 56 parents across the country about this very issue. Collectively, they sent 74 children off to college between 2017 and 2024.
Most parents of college-bound young people know there is a sexual assault problem on campus, but they do not see it as a problem that is likely to affect their child or children, my research shows.
Relying too much on rape myths

The problem of campus sexual assault is well documented. Almost 1 in 4 undergraduate women, 1 in 20 undergraduate men, and nearly 1 in 4 transgender and gender-diverse young people report experiencing sexual assault while in college.
Almost 11% of undergraduate men have committed sexual assault, according to one estimate. Almost 80% of campus sexual assaults go unreported.

This disconnect can be explained by the fact that most of the parents I spoke to unconsciously rely on rape myths to understand campus sexual assault. Rape myths refer to widely held and inaccurate beliefs about rape, rapists and rape victims that serve to deny, justify or downplay sexual assault.
Most parents of sons I spoke with, for instance, said that their son is not the kind of person who would jump out from behind a bush wielding a weapon and attack a young woman walking alone at night.

Campus sexual assault is rarely perpetrated by an armed stranger. More often, it is committed by someone who knows the victim. In most campus sexual assaults, as well, the victim and the perpetrator know one another, a pattern known as date rape or acquaintance rape.

While most parents are convinced that their son will never assault someone, and they rarely consider that he could be the victim of a sexual assault, my research finds that in the face of the widespread problem of campus sexual assault, parents of sons are overwhelmingly concerned that their son might be falsely accused.

Out of the 38 parents of sons in my sample, 58% expressed concern that their son risked being falsely accused of sexual assault. This aligns with the myth that women lie about being assaulted for revenge or attention, among other reasons.
Approximately 5% to 10% of reported sexual assaults are false accusations, according to research.
One mother, who has two sons and one daughter, described “a fear that your son will be falsely accused.”
“That should not be my biggest priority, but it is in my head, knowing my kid,” she said.
Not thinking their daughters might be at risk

Perhaps more surprisingly, my research found that many parents of daughters did not view them as being at risk of sexual violence, even when they understood the extent of the problem of campus sexual assault.
Many parents of daughters responded to questions about whether they educated their child or children about sexual assault prevention by stating, “I didn’t have to worry about that.”
Some explained that their daughter’s specific personality traits protected her from being victimized – especially if she was strong, outspoken, level-headed or had “street smarts.”
If their daughter was religious, did not drink alcohol or use drugs before going to college, or was queer, parents felt she was not at risk of being assaulted.

I spoke with one mother with a son and a daughter in college. She said she was not worried about her daughter being sexually assaulted because her daughter “will for sure fight to take care of herself. … She’s always been very strong like that.”

Another mother with one daughter in college said she was not worried because her daughter doesn’t drink or want to have sex before marriage. “I feel comfortable. She is not getting into situations that could lead to something,” she said.
Such thinking aligns with the false belief that women are responsible for their own sexual victimization, especially if they drink or use recreational drugs.
Talking to kids about sexual assault

For many parents, conversations with their children about sexuality-related topics are difficult. These conversations require that parents see their child as a sexual being or a soon-to-be sexually active person, which is, admittedly, not easy for a lot of parents.
But this kind of conversation can help protect them from possible harm.
First, parents could educate themselves about the reality of campus sexual assault.

Parents I spoke to often used their own collegiate experiences to understand campus sexual assault. I heard people saying that if they did not know anyone who was sexually assaulted in college, it must not have been a problem on their campus.
The next step is to take one’s knowledge about campus sexual assault and share it, over time, in ongoing conversations with their child or children.
These sorts of conversations should go beyond phrases like “no means no” and include discussions about affirmative consent, clear communication, reading body language and power dynamics.
Consent education is just the beginning.
I have found that many parents believe that the values they taught their child, or children, would magically translate into their child or children never perpetrating sexual violence.
Not an easy talk, but a necessary one

I thought one of the most alarming aspects of the Cornell gang-rape case was that one of the fraternity brothers sent a message to a Chi Phi group chat, announcing that Jane Doe was sexually available to anyone who was interested. None of the 50 fraternity brothers who saw this message stepped in to stop the alleged gang rape or help Jane Doe get out of harm’s way.

My research shows that parents expressed fears surrounding the influence of technology on young people but mostly worried about sexting and revenge porn, particularly when their children were younger.

Speaking with teenagers and young adults about sexual assault is not easy. However, when considering the parents of the Cornell seven and the unnamed victim, there are far more uncomfortable positions for a parent to be in.

articles.title: Faculty and students show how reporting is done when a university partners with local news
articles.author: Teri Finneman, Professor of Journalism, University of Kansas
paras: Catherine Bilskie, the advertising and office manager for the newspaper in Solon, Iowa, had seen many local news outlets close. So she was sure her job at the Solon Economist was about to go one Friday morning in February 2024.

But to her surprise, a new owner, Jason Brummond, appeared. He not only promised to keep her and her co-worker employed at the weekly paper but assured them raises if they agreed to an unusual new venture. And he wasn’t a wealthy benefactor or a representative from a private equity firm – he came from the University of Iowa.

It’s just one example of academic institutions stepping up to address the “news desert” crisis: Thousands of communities across the U.S. have lost local newspapers over the past two decades. And journalism faculty, staff and students are increasingly working together to either rescue legacy newspapers or start new publications for communities lacking local news outlets.

These partnerships have ranged from the Spanish-language news site Noticiero Móvil at the University of Nevada, Reno, to “Good Morning Indian Country” at the University of Kansas, to The Scope at Northeastern in Boston.

We’re journalism professors who have studied and experienced the opportunities and challenges of running community news through higher education. Our new book, “News Desert U,” asks whether this approach is one solution to saving local news. We believe the need is urgent given the stakes and the scope of the crisis.
These experiments come against a grim backdrop.

Over 3,000 newspapers have closed in the U.S. in the past 20 years, including about 170 in 2025, according to Northwestern’s 2026 State of Local News report. Causes include an antiquated business model, declining advertising revenue and hedge-fund buyouts that have gutted papers. Northwestern’s 2025 report estimated that total print newspaper circulation has declined 70% in the past 20 years.
But university partnerships can show promise, we found, with the help of the next generation of journalists.

Iowa’s Solon Economist is one example. The University of Iowa doesn’t actually own the paper, or its sister paper, the Mount Vernon-Lisbon Sun. Still, the relationship is key to making the new venture work.

Its owner, Brummond, is also the publisher of the University of Iowa’s student newspaper, the Daily Iowan, which is owned and operated by the nonprofit Student Publications. While the student newspaper office is inside the journalism school’s building, it operates independently.

In August 2023, Student Publications began talks about buying the Sun and the Economist after the weeklies’ then owner reached out about selling the publications. With both newspapers 20-30 minutes from campus, discussions included how the faculty and students could help the papers.

The Journalism School’s director, Melissa Tully, was immediately in favor – provided that the newspapers’ existing professional staff stay and not be replaced with students. In addition to the editors, this included keeping the advertising and circulation staff.

“They know these communities. So that was really important just from a moral and ethical imperative, but also from a news perspective,” she said. “They’re trusted in their communities. They know what’s going on.”

Student Publications bought both newspapers for US$10,000 in 2024. Since then, circulation has remained stable at both, Brummond said, even as many other publications across the country have suffered declines.
Meanwhile, students in classes such as community news, high school sports, social media marketing and photography contribute for academic credit while other students do paid internships.
Solon Economist Editor Chris Umscheid said he welcomes a revolving door of student interns because it means he’s “actually going to have staff for once.”
“People thought we were going to be the university’s paper, and we’re not,” he said. “I don’t anticipate anything changing there. We’re still going to focus on everything Solon that we can.”

The success has led to Student Publications getting requests to buy other newspapers, Tully said, and it’s working on a list of criteria to consider future partnerships. Brummond cautions these arrangements aren’t easy to pull off, as they require a careful review of finances, workflow and logistical complications that come with a merger.
Liz King, who served as Solon Public Library director, said many locals were afraid the newspaper would close, which would have been a hard blow for the town of about 3,000.
Some readers only get their news through the newspaper, she said. “They’re not comfortable with online sources.”
Dink NeSmith had a similar close scare in Georgia with the The Oglethorpe Echo.

Owner Ralph Maxwell had decided in September 2021 that he had no choice but to shutter the paper due to his own health issues, revenue declines and lack of interest from prospective buyers. He gave NeSmith, an old friend and retired newspaper owner, an early heads-up.
“I don’t know that I want to live in a town that doesn’t have its newspaper,” was NeSmith’s response. He told Maxwell: “You can’t close the Echo.”
NeSmith immediately reached out to the University of Georgia’s journalism school to suggest a partnership.

In the meantime, NeSmith worked to set up a separate nonprofit, Oglethorpe Echo Legacy, for the paper’s new ownership structure. Keeping the newspaper’s finances independent of the university was an important step to ensure the paper would not be subject to any possible “whims” of future administrations, as Charles Davis, the journalism school’s dean, put it. That status was also a signal to Oglethorpe County that the paper’s goal was to serve the community, not make money, he added.
The new nonprofit bought the paper from Maxwell in October 2021 for $10 – a check that Maxwell never cashed and has since been framed.

Davis asked Andy Johnston, an adjunct professor with decades of journalism experience, to serve as the newspaper’s full-time editor. Since November 2021, Johnston has led a team of journalism faculty and students, with the help of several adult staff and volunteers from the county.

The paper covers a wide terrain. Oglethorpe County has over 16,000 people stretching over 442 square miles, and Lexington, where the Echo has its office, is 18 miles (29 kilometers) from the campus in Athens. The reporting staff is provided by journalism professor Amanda Bright’s capstone class – 20 students each semester. Supplementary funding comes from the journalism school, various grants and Echo subscription and advertising funds.

She pairs two students to each beat, with one in charge of a story and the other in charge of editing and producing, with a rotation each week. Students need to turn in eight stories a semester – with corresponding editing and producing assignments that include video, an email newsletter and social media – to get class credit.

When the journalism school took over, the weekly had only a printed newspaper, with no website, social media presence or other digital products, she said. So in their first print edition, the editors outlined their plan for the newspaper to readers and then introduced the student reporters, which they still do every semester.

The partnership has paid off. Print subscriptions to The Echo have doubled and overall digital audience has quadrupled thanks to the launch of new digital products, Bright said. Advertising revenue, meanwhile, has tripled, she said. However, it took some time for local businesses to get used to advertising again, NeSmith said.

But many challenges remain. Johnston has to handle student turnover every semester while students covering events such as government meetings face a steep learning curve and need support. The additional time it takes to edit student copy means content doesn’t appear as quickly. Many faculty members have to work long hours to keep the paper afloat.
But the broader impact is clear: More than two dozen students have gone into local news as a career following their time at the Echo, Bright said.

Should other universities want to follow this model, they need at least two key people in leadership, whether that’s two faculty members or one from faculty and a professional editor, Bright said. “That’s a bottom-line necessity for sanity,” she added.
One common theme from our research is that a service-oriented approach to news that addresses the community’s needs takes priority over profit at these partnerships.

The built-in advantages for these initiatives is that the faculty and staff who tend to manage them get their paychecks and health insurance from their university work. They don’t need to draw a living wage from the news outlet’s finances.

These partnerships are also ideal for students seeking real-world experience while earning class credit or internship wages. And journalism schools are already stocked with multimedia equipment that students can use for their reporting.

Still, they can look deceptively simple on the surface, Brummond said. Tully, at the University of Iowa, recommends other interested universities should go slowly. Building a successful project takes patient experimentation and a willingness to regroup when needed, in her view.
“Doing this slowly is OK,” she said. “In the end, it’s going to be better. So far, that’s been a good recipe for us.”
Teri Finneman and Pamela Walck are co-authors of the book "News Desert U."

Pamela E. Walck does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: School librarians are vanishing from Michigan schools just when they are needed most
articles.author: Shannon Oltmann, Associate Dean of Information Sciences, Wayne State University
paras: Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools report having a school library staffed with a trained school librarian.

Although Michigan strongly recommends that schools employ certified librarians, the state does not require them. In the 2023–24 school year, the state ranked 46th in the student-to-librarian ratio, with one school librarian for every 2,760 students.

The lack of school librarians impacts students across Michigan, but particularly in low-income communities like Detroit and Flint and more isolated ones like Alcona County in the northern Lower Peninsula and Ontonagon in the Upper Peninsula, exacerbating disparities in resources for young people.

We are scholars in library and information sciences from Wayne State University, studying information access and ethics and equity in education and school libraries. Currently, we are conducting a statewide campaign to contact every school in Michigan and learn about their libraries, staffing, book collections, technology resources and more.

Michigan’s 2025–26 School Aid budget funded our statewide survey to measure the school librarian shortage and guide efforts to address it. Our work, and the work of many others, reveals how school librarians help students become strong readers and informed citizens.
Catalysts for student achievement

A missing librarian is harder to see than an empty bookshelf. A room full of books can look like a school library. But if students cannot borrow those books, teachers have no librarian to plan lessons with, and no one leads author visits or digital citizenship lessons, the space offers only a fraction of what a school library can provide.

School librarians bring those services to life. Also called school library media specialists, they hold a teaching certificate and complete advanced education. They connect students with books they want to read and work with teachers to build richer lessons, using library resources to extend learning beyond the textbook.

Their impact stretches far beyond standardized test scores, though studies link strong library programs with higher student achievement and improved student literacy, especially for struggling readers. They can instill a love of reading and teach technological skills, which is critical in the age of artificial intelligence.

At our Michigan School Census symposium held in 2026, Michigan school librarians and a principal described what that work looks like. Brian Peck, a teacher librarian at Detroit’s UPrep Academy, helped students research and build a library where none had existed. He reported that 334 students voluntarily visited and checked out books during the previous school year.

At West Ottawa, librarian Julia Reynolds described replacing crowded shelves with displays that let children see book covers. Circulation quadrupled, she reported. A principal on the panel explained how district support helped schools make library visits a priority from the first week of school.
Students’ information worlds
Access to information is only a start. Students also need help making sense of what reaches them through searches, social media and AI.
AI can create convincing fake videos of students doing or saying things they never did, harming their reputations and undermining trust in what people see online.

Less visible forces shape students’ information worlds, too. Algorithms and online platforms often dictate which search results and suggested videos appear first. Students need to understand that the first result is not necessarily the most credible or trustworthy source. AI is becoming so prominent that even elementary school students are learning about it.
Building information literacy
Information literacy means knowing how to find, judge and use information. School librarians turn those skills into practice.
For a history assignment, a librarian might help students compare a newspaper account with a firsthand record. Who produced each source? What might explain their different accounts?
The same habits apply to AI. Students can trace a claim to its source, check whether the source exists and compare what it says with the generated answer. A confident response still needs evidence.

Guided by certified school librarians, students can build upon these foundations and learn to effectively find, evaluate and use information, including news articles about a historic event for a social studies assignment or to analyze current social media trends. Students can also judge the accuracy, recency and relevance of information. They learn to apply information in decision-making, writing and other forms of communication.
Becoming savvy digital citizens
Knowing whether information is trustworthy is an important skill. Deciding what to do with it is another.
Digital citizenship includes deciding whether to post someone’s photo, seeking their permission before doing so, and choosing not to share a fake video.
Recent research emphasizes that digital citizenship prepares students to be empowered online and act ethically, safely and legally in digital environments.
Our work also starts with the knowledge young people bring to school.

Project Restoring Urban School Libraries helped classroom teachers earn the additional endorsement needed to become school librarians. The program combined mentoring with coursework that drew on students’ cultures, including using hip-hop to explore how young people find, create and share information.
Students start by examining the media they already use. A lesson might ask them to trace a sample, credit its creator and discuss what changes when someone else’s work reaches a new audience.

Principal preparation programs can help school leaders understand what school librarians contribute beyond book checkout. But principals and school librarians often train in separate academic units: colleges of education and schools of library and information science. Without shared coursework or joint projects, principals may complete their training without learning how to work with a school librarian.

In our “Closing the Literacy Gap” symposium, we brought school librarians and administrators together on a panel to show what their partnerships make possible. West Ottawa Principal Audra Bolhuis joined school librarian Julia Reynolds and compared a librarian to “an instructional coach.” She described someone teachers can turn to for resources and help with classroom projects, extending the librarian’s role beyond students’ scheduled library visits.
School library jobs remain vulnerable to budget cuts, and the number of school librarians across the state has been decreasing since 2010.

To understand what schools provide and where support is missing, we launched the state-funded Michigan School Census in September 2026. By Oct. 21, 1,054 schools – about one-third of those invited – had completed it. Our public response map tracks participation across districts.

Schools without libraries or librarians are essential to painting the full picture: Their staff can explain how students get books and research help when those services are absent. The findings will guide recommendations for staffing, resources and funding.
Counting what schools have is the first step toward deciding what every Michigan student should be able to count on.

I am Associate Dean/Director of the School of Information Sciences at Wayne State University, which received an appropriation from the Michigan Legislature in 2025. The funding was routed through the Michigan Department of Education, to Wayne State University, then to my School. I do not benefit directly from funding (i.e., no income). Second, I am a recipient of a current National Leadership Grant from the Institute of Museum and Library Services, for $445,000. This grant funds research to study how public libraries respond to censorship.
