articles.title: How Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library is helping kids start reading when they’re very young
articles.author: Alex H. Poole, Associate Professor of Information Science, Drexel University
paras: By the time Dolly Parton died on Aug. 25, 2026, her Imagination Library had gifted more than 332 million children’s books to babies and kids in all 50 states and four other countries: Canada, the U.K., Australia and Ireland.
If they were set end to end, these books would circle the earth 1.8 times.

This free program mails an age-appropriate book monthly to each enrolled child from birth to age 5, meaning up to 60 books will fill these children’s shelves by the time they graduate from the program.

Though a selection committee tweaks the lists annually, each participant receives Watty Piper’s “The Little Engine That Could” as their first book and Nancy Carlson’s “Look Out Kindergarten, Here I Come!” as their last.

I’m an information science professor who studies reading behavior. In my research for an upcoming academic article about the Imagination Library, I’ve found that its free monthly books help families develop children’s literacy, prepare children for kindergarten and encourage a lifelong love of reading.
Emphasis on early literacy

Parton, most remembered as a popular country singer, embraced many musical genres during her long and successful career in show business. She was also a songwriter, entrepreneur, actor and philanthropist.

She created this program because she, like most early childhood literacy experts, believed that reading begins in the home. That is, parents and other guardians are a child’s first teachers, and reading aloud to children contributes to their future literacy.
First graders who struggle with reading usually continue to have trouble with literacy later on.

Very young children in lower-income households generally have less access to books and hear fewer words than higher-income kids. This class-based difference may lead to disparities in reading skills later on.

Like Parton, who was born in a one-bedroom cabin in an Appalachian region of Tennessee that had neither running water nor electricity, the Imagination Library’s origins were modest. It started in her hometown, hardscrabble Sevier County, in late 1995. Its initial order of 1,760 books was destined for the children who lived where she grew up.
The program came from “a very serious place in my heart,” Parton once said. On many occasions, she emphasized how her own father’s illiteracy inspired her to found it – with him.

“Daddy couldn’t read nor write, and it always just seemed to cripple him, and he was embarrassed about it,” Parton told American Libraries in 2018. “My daddy just loved it when all the little kids would call me ‘The Book Lady,’” she said later.

In contrast, Parton was a bookworm. “I always loved books,” she explained in an interview. “I don’t remember learning to read, it was just something I always did. That’s how I knew there was a world beyond the Smoky Mountains.”
Parton’s Dollywood Foundation covers overhead and administrative expenses, coordinates the book selection committee, maintains the book order system and arranges orders and fulfillment.
The Imagination Library is available to any child in a community participating in the program, regardless of their family’s income.

To be eligible, a community must secure a local partner. Local partners publicize the program and enroll children. They have to pay US$2.60 per month per child to defray costs of purchasing books wholesale and mailing them. These partners include schools, public libraries and government agencies, and several kinds of nonprofits, including foundations.
Nonpartisan expert committees of educators and librarians select the books, nearly all published by Penguin Random House.

The program is continuing under the direction of the Dollywood Foundation’s president, Jeff Conyers. A Penguin Random House vice president said, “We will continue that work with the utmost pride and care, just as we know she would have wanted.”
But funding challenges have arisen in at least four states.
Steady growth and diversification

By 2001, the Imagination Library had expanded to affiliates in nearly a dozen states. The next year, it extended its reach to 92 Native American communities, partnering with the Cherokee Nation, the Bureau of Indian Affairs, Parents as Teachers and the National Center for Family Literacy.
In late 2003, the Imagination Library mailed its one-millionth book. In 2004, it launched its first statewide program – fittingly, in Tennessee.

It added bilingual titles in Spanish and English in 2003 and launched a bilingual Spanish website in 2022. The Imagination Library also supplied audio and braille books for those who needed them beginning in 2011.

Parton celebrated when the library mailed its 100-millionth book in 2018. “We never thought it would be this big,” she told NPR. “I just wanted to do something great for my dad and for my home county and, at the most, maybe a couple of counties over. But then it just took wings of its own.”

The Imagination Library shipped its 200-millionth book in 2023 and its 300-millionth book in 2025. By 2024, 1 in 7 children under the age of 5 in the United States were receiving books for free every month, courtesy of this initiative.

Other programs give free books to young children, including Reach Out and Read in the U.S., which since 1989 has handed them out at children’s medical checkups. Bookstart, which launched in 1992, offers every baby in England, Wales and Northern Ireland a free book and tips on reading aloud to kids.
Parents and caregivers highly praise the program.
Many studies have found that children get excited about getting their own books in the mail, addressed to them personally. Both they and their families also take great pride in book ownership.
“A lot of (children) wait at the mailbox at the first of the month,” Parton told The Washington Post. “They think that I bring the book myself, like I’m Santa Claus.”
As one parent told an education researcher, “We read the books when they come in the mail instead of watching TV.”

The library’s books “nudge” children to make reading a regular habit. Many studies have found that children who are read to more frequently by their loved ones, spend more time reading together daily and ask more frequently for books to be read to them.

This program aims not only to boost a child’s love of reading but to improve their cognitive development and get them ready for elementary school by enlarging their vocabulary and improving their listening skills.

Kids who get the books tend to know more letters, understand how books and printed words work, recognize and retain words’ sounds, and both understand and use more spoken words. Similarly, children enrolled in the program have scored higher than their peers when they take a standard kindergarten entrance early-reading skills test.
In line with Parton’s original goal, the Imagination Library may do the most to change reading habits in lower-income homes – where children’s books tend to be scarce.

articles.title: Using an AI chatbot to practice new languages can be helpful, but it doesn’t replace speaking with an actual person
articles.author: Antonio Perez-Nunez, Associate Professor of Spanish, College of Charleston
paras: Approximately 30% of U.S. adults who were learning a language in 2025 reported that they were using artificial intelligence as a resource.

People can use AI-powered chatbots, like ChatGPT and Gemini, to practice conversations in other languages, ask what an unfamiliar phrase means or get feedback on their writing. These apps and websites also offer voice features for speaking and listening in another language.
But can someone learn a language with a chatbot alone?
Research suggests that these tools can help learners build language skills, but there isn’t evidence that strictly using these apps is enough to become fluent in another language.
That said, they can still offer a helping hand. Learning another language involves understanding what you hear and read, as well as knowing how to express yourself verbally and in writing.
I study how chatbots can help someone practice these four skills in different ways.
What learners can gain from chatbots depends on how they use them.
Chatbots can help build language proficiency

First, people can use the voice features in chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini to role-play conversations and practice speaking about different topics. People can practice for a job interview by answering questions about their experience, asking for feedback and trying different ways of expressing an unfamiliar phrase.

Research suggests that practicing speaking with chatbots can help language learners become more fluent and accurate. People can repeat a conversation and try again after receiving feedback from the chatbot, giving them time and perhaps the confidence to work on unfamiliar expressions and recurring mistakes.

Speaking another language can be stressful, especially when people worry about making mistakes in front of someone else. Some language learners report finding chatbot conversations less intimidating than interactions with people, and feeling they can experiment without worrying about being judged.
Not being self-conscious may make people more willing to speak and keep practicing after they make a mistake.

Chatbots can also support people as they draft a sentence or a paragraph in another language, and offer them feedback and revisions. Research suggests that these tools can help identify grammar errors and improve sentence structure and clarity. Immediate feedback can also encourage learners to revise more often.

But the quality of the feedback that chatbots offer varies. A review of 51 studies on AI feedback in second-language writing found that this kind of feedback could contain errors or misinterpret the writer’s intended meaning. Some studies also reported that learners relied too heavily on AI, taking less control over decisions about their own writing.

Chatbots work best, then, when learners consider which individual suggestions to use and why. For example, they can check whether a suggested change preserves their intended meaning, or ask a chatbot why it was recommended and try using what they learned from the feedback in a new sentence.

People could also ask a voice-enabled chatbot to tell a short story or ask questions, then request that it repeat or rephrase anything they do not understand. In a study of university students in China, language learners practiced listening with ChatGPT and received feedback on their answers outside their regular English classes. Their English listening test scores improved more than those of students who used teacher-provided materials for that additional practice.

Finally, chatbots can help someone work through difficult reading material in a foreign language. Research suggests that reading a simplified version first may help learners grasp the main idea and work out unfamiliar words.
Chatbots can help people develop some language skills, but they still lack the cultural understanding, lived experience and emotional support that actual human beings bring to a conversation.
For starters, chatbots may reflect cultural biases.

A study of 10 language models compared their answers about the importance of work and religion, among other values, with human survey responses. The chatbots’ answers were generally closer to those of people from the Netherlands, Germany, the United States and Japan, even when asked to respond as someone from India or China.

Some responses also relied on stereotypes. Asked to imagine an ideal job for a Dutch person, Gemini suggested leading bicycle tours past cheese factories, windmills and tulip fields. For language learners, this raises concerns that a chatbot may provide cultural information that is inaccurate, biased or oversimplified.

Privacy matters, too. Companies providing chatbot services may record learners’ text and voice data. Practicing a job interview with real details about an employer, for example, could involve sharing confidential information with a chatbot.
In a survey published in 2025, students who reported more positive experiences with chatbots also worried more about feeling disconnected from other people and lacking emotional support.

In language learning, a 2026 study of 10 English teachers and 10 students at a university in Turkey explored their experiences using AI in the classroom. Some found it useful for teaching and learning, but their accounts also emphasized the importance of connecting with people.

Existing research on using chatbots to learn a language also has limits. Studies in one review tested activities lasting from a single learning session to about four months of practice. Most studies involve adults, and English is by far the most studied language.
Longer studies involving different ages of learners and an array of languages would help establish whether the benefits last and how widely they apply.

As chatbots become more widely used, educators can help students evaluate their responses and make their own decisions about how to use them. For example, a teacher might ask students to write a draft, get feedback from a chatbot and explain why they accepted, adapted or rejected its suggestions.
Teachers also build relationships based on trust and an understanding of students’ needs. They might talk through a difficult task with a discouraged student and offer encouragement to keep going.

Teachers need training to make effective use of chatbots. This includes understanding how they work, recognizing their limitations and learning to design and select activities that meet students’ learning needs.

Chatbots offer new ways to practice a language and build skills, but the evidence does not yet show that they are enough on their own. For now, their clearest value may be offering new opportunities to learn alongside teachers and other speakers.
Antonio Perez-Nunez is the owner of Lingua Innova LLC. Outside of academia, he developed a chatbot-based platform for conversation practice that is owned by Vista Higher Learning.

articles.title: Why Trump’s plan to cut Head Start regulations could undermine services for the country’s poorest families
articles.author: Alexander Thim, PhD Candidate of Economics, UMass Amherst; Westfield State University
paras: For over 60 years, the federal program Head Start has helped children from low-income families get ready for elementary school through early childhood education and related support services, like speech therapy and developmental screenings.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced on Aug. 6, 2026, proposed changes that would cut the majority of the rules that guide Head Start programs and would also give states more authority over how the federal program is run.

This proposal comes after the Trump administration tried unsuccessfully to defund Head Start in 2025. Funding freezes and the government shutdown in 2025 also caused many Head Start centers to temporarily close. These closures caused some staff to resign and compelled some Head Start families to withdraw their children from the program.

The latest proposed changes could alter the program’s day-to-day operations in various ways – whether that means no longer giving children free daily meals or relaxing the program’s student-to-teacher ratio requirements.
The new rules would also mandate that all classes be taught in English, regardless of the language children and their families speak at home.

Some Head Start participants, workers and advocates have expressed concern that these changes would transform Head Start into a different program – from one that alleviates the effects of poverty to one that has a more generic emphasis on early childhood education.
As a doctoral candidate in economics, I’ve spent the past six years studying Head Start and its impact on local communities.

Head Start is a vital provider of childcare and other services for the poorest children and their families in rural, urban and suburban communities across the U.S. Reducing the number of federal rules governing Head Start will likely not enhance the quality or broaden the availability of the program to the children and families who need it most.
Understanding Head Start’s launch

Head Start is a free, nationwide year-round preschool program that serves more than 700,000 low-income children ages 3-5 and their families. It operates with a US$12.3 billion annual budget. Head Start providers are typically run by nonprofits or local schools.

Eligibility for the program is generally determined based on household income, though there are some categories of children who are automatically eligible, such those who are unhoused or in foster care.
The majority of Head Start participants attend preschools run by one of the 17,000 Head Start centers across the country. Some home-based services are also offered to support families.

Head Start is notable among early childhood education programs because it provides more than just free childcare and education. Head Start is required to serve at least two meals per day to the young children who attend these schools, as well as offer speech therapy and other kinds of developmental support and health services when needed.
In some rural communities, Head Start’s ability to bring dentists and doctors to centers has dramatically expanded healthcare access for entire towns or school districts.

Many states and cities have introduced or expanded their own free public preschool options in recent years. But Head Start continues to be an essential early childcare program for low-income children and their families across the country.
President Lyndon B. Johnson’s administration launched Head Start in 1965 as an eight-week summer preschool program.

Over 500,000 low-income children participated in Head Start during this first summer. The program quickly proved popular and effective. The government then expanded the program to cover the entire school year, starting in the fall of 1965.

The early childhood experts who designed Head Start understood that simply offering free education to low-income children was not enough to offset the impacts of growing up in poverty. They recognized the necessity of a comprehensive, whole-child approach, a philosophy that continues to define the program today.

So while Head Start primarily provides education and childcare services, the program also requires parents to participate in parent-child activities and other activities that engage families across their broader communities.

Since 1965, other programs have been introduced under the Head Start umbrella, including Early Head Start, which provides Head Start services to children from birth to 3 years old, as well as pregnant women.
Overall, more than 40 million children have participated in Head Start since its launch.
Head Start’s impact on children
Numerous studies have analyzed how Head Start affects children who participate in the program, as well as their families.

Much of the research has found that Head Start’s positive effects on its participants are sustained through the end of third grade. These effects include significantly improved educational and health outcomes.

Researchers have also found that participating in Head Start lowered the likelihood of being placed in special education or committing a crime, and it lowered child mortality rates, among other positive results.
Head Start’s longer-term impacts, meaning those measured over the course of a child’s lifetime, are less clear.

Some studies have found impacts that last well into adulthood, though some have not. These studies contribute to the debate over the benefits of Head Start “fading out” over time, though the causes and significance of this phenomenon are disputed.

One notable study that Congress commissioned in 2010 found positive effects for Head Start participants in cognitive, social-emotional and health outcomes, though few of these impacts lasted through the end of first grade.

Both the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank, and the Trump administration have cited this report to argue that Head Start is ineffective. However, it is important to note that many scholars have pointed to significant problems with the methodology of the study.

The Trump administration suggests that these changes will cut costs by $1.5 billion to $3 billion by 2031. Those savings would account for roughly 0.04% of any given year’s typical total federal budget.

I believe that these proposed changes fly in the face of Head Start’s goals, and changes to Head Start’s rules and standards will likely contribute to the existing issues of inconsistent access to Head Start across the country.

The Administration for Children and Families, an office within the Department of Health and Human Services, is accepting public comments on the changes, as required by federal law. It will review the comments after the Oct. 6, 2026, deadline.
As of late September, there were over 18,465 comments, most expressing serious concern about these changes.
